text: Thank you, Judita and Eva, for the invitation to present in your session
on building resilient data infrastructures for biodiversity science.
I am the maintainer of Bionomia, which combines automation and
volunteerism to facilitate the creation and maintenance of
more than 50 million attributable connections between biodiversity
records and human expertise. Its interface has been
translated into seven languages through the generous efforts of
linguists on Crowdin.
Bionomia receives modest daily human traffic with
occasional hourly spikes in the tens of thousands of people and is
generally manageable with a cloud-based technical
infrastructure across root-level access to three
adequately provisioned virtual machines on DigitalOcean for
database asset resizing and caching and search or
programmatic API usage, as well as a job queue on
Redis to orchestrate long-running tasks.
However, Bionomia has faced challenges from multiple sources,
including many you see here. Some, like code maintenance
and server upkeep, have well-known solutions.
Others, like institutional oversight, for instance,
raise persistent questions about its relationship with my
employer, particularly when there are spikes in its
international visibility.
More recently, misbehaving bots and AI crawlers
have significantly degraded performance, taking down the website
on dozens of occasions.
Mercifully, Cloudflare now acts as a gatekeeper
to thwart most of these AI crawlers, and I can quickly
adjust fine-grained new actions, such as blocking whole
countries from access, while I develop more appropriate solutions
to stymie bad actors.
But I worry about the long-term sustainability of Cloudflare itself
and its relationship with a global
web community.
In addition to RESTful API and reconciliation
endpoints that do not participate in these Cloudflare
filters,
the code base is made more resilient through the encapsulation
of core functions into high-performant standalone libraries
of code, such as a RubyGem, now ported into
Go for the parsing of human names, as is typically
expressed in Darwin Core terms.
Once a month, a graph structure in CSV form is
produced and then zipped up and pushed into Zenodo, an
industry-standard archive.
In theory, one could build a triplestore from this structure, and I welcome
those who may wish to do so.
Likewise, Bionomia auto-archives a CSV-based
frictionless data package to Zenodo every month for each of
the roughly 9,000 data sets that share their data to GBIF.
Each package contains unique lists of people identified
by their ORCID or Wikidata Q numbers, relationally
linked to one-to-many occurrence records to express whether they collected
or identified those specimens, as well as files that
identify logically incongruent records, such as those
whose values for collection date fall
before a collector's date of birth or after their death.
Volunteer scribes, as they're called in Bionomia, create and
maintain these links between GBIF occurrence records and
those industry-recognized expressions of identity for
collectors and determiners as either ORCID IDs or
Wikidata Q numbers. The expectation is that data
providers to GBIF, like herbaria and museums, may,
at their leisure, examine and incorporate these new
data enhancements into their local stores, thus completing a
data round trip, and many now do.
For instance, staff at the Natural History Museum at the University of
Oslo use these frictionless data packages to fill new
gaps as they digitize new records, then share the
Wikidata and ORCID identifiers directly to GBIF in
purpose-built Darwin Core terms.
Individual researchers also participate in archiving their
occurrence records, as shown on GBIF, through integration between
Bionomia and Zenodo. Here, Sabina has a data site
DOI, you can see at the bottom left on this figure in a badge,
and a formatted citation, and she puts these into her curriculum
vitae.
In summary, relatively small niche projects may
be resilient in the short term within a landscape of
large-scale, well-funded biodiversity infrastructure if they
acknowledge and plan for decommissioning at the outset.
That perspective results in laser focus on
simplicity for the data schema, the website code,
search algorithms, and when to say no to new features.
Counterintuitively, it also means finding ways to eliminate any
technical debt others may incur by using the
products of what may be a short-lived project.
Reusable libraries of code in multiple programming languages
and distributed and versioned data archives in multiple forms
help reduce that technical debt and, in turn,
actually create more generous, welcoming environments
in which to work.
I am grateful to the volunteers in Bionomia who have each carved
out a vision of their own, the translators who have helped create a more
universally accessible environment, the Biological Collections in
Ecology and Evolution network for their support, and to
Andrea, Sean, and Tonell, whose leadership has resulted
in well-attended workshops throughout botany meetings in the United States,
